articles.title: Climate warming can slow how tree roots feed soil microbes
articles.description: A plant's roots do much of their work out of sight, pulling in water and nutrients and holding the plant in place. That makes it hard to see how plants respond when conditions underground change, and how a warming climate affects them. New Dartmouth-led studies look at the strategies plants use below the surface to adapt and survive.

articles.title: The end of deadlines
articles.description: I have a love-hate relationship with deadlines. Like many of us, I have long dreamed of the day when the endless stream of homework assignments would finally cease, and I would be freed from the tyranny of Friday 11:59 p.m. Canvas submissions forever. Yet as I sit here typing out this article at 11 p.m. the day it is due, I also recognize that there are times I simply wouldn't get things done without them. All of my life I have been a perpetual procrastinator. However, while I was in school, last-minute panic made sure that I always turned in my assignments on time, even if sometimes I cut it a little close. Heavens forbid I miss a deadline and immediately feel my stomach drop as I see "MISSING" in big red letters alongside a drop in my course grade. I am currently in the second year of my master's here at Hopkins. Having finished all of my coursework in my first year left with just independent research and thesis-writing, I have finally reached the promised land and not had to open Canvas a single time this semester. While I still have proposal submission dates and project timelines - and will for the rest of my working career once I graduate and get a job - traditional deadlines in the way I have known for the last 17 years are finally behind me. But now that the day has dawned, this end of deadlines doesn't feel like the triumphant happy ending I always imagined. For one thing, while the incessant bombarding of small deadlines fades away, the few deadlines that remain are more important and less forgiving. It is no longer a few percentages off of your course grades that just means you need to study harder for the next exam. It is missing a grant application that sets you back a year, or a job application posting when you don't know when the next one will come. Yet even more dangerous are the aspects for which there is no explicit deadline at all: exercising regularly, spending time with your loved ones and pursuing your personal goals. Without the structure of deadlines to help me navigate my life, I all too often find myself paralyzed by the expansive fields of endless possibility and overwhelming choices. Deadlines are annoying, but annoyance is the point of an alarm. In their absence, I feel lost, directionless. The harder truth is, even for these aspects of life, deadlines don't disappear, they simply become invisible. For most people, there is a double-digit number of summers that you will experience in your lifetime. And while it is never too late to chase your dreams, waiting around forever to start may mean you never get the chance to achieve them. From calling your mom to spending time with that friend you don't know will move away in two years, there still exists a "deadline." The difference is that there is no demarcated date you are made aware of until it is too late and you realize the real deadline passed months ago. So while my break from deadlines has been nice, I no longer think I want it to last forever. In place of an end to deadlines, perhaps I simply need to re-wire my relationship with deadlines. Instead of thinking of them as stressful evaluations, I should think of them as checkpoints of progress to help me on my way to what I want. A gentle reminder that time moves onwards, and of a promise I made to a future self. And once there's no more professor to set deadlines for me, I will have to find other ways to create them, like asking my friends to help keep me accountable. As I move more fully into post-grad life and adulthood - a world where reminders aren't automatic and the path forward is less conspicuous than ever - I will need to learn new strategies to self-motivate and spur myself to action in lieu of the adrenaline of last-minute panic. My hope is that one day I can live life to the fullest and chase my dreams relentlessly without the need for a Canvas notification pinging me a reminder to seize the day. But until then, deadlines can help keep me on track and remind me of the things I decide matter most. Jason Chang is a graduate student from Woodbury, Minn. studying Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering. His column is a celebration of the quiet moments that linger amid the jumble of our busy lives: moments of stillness, reflection and a space to just exist.

articles.title: In the Search for Exoplanets, Some Failures Are A Success
articles.description: Astronomers used decades of archival data and new radial velocity measurements to search for exoplanets around a neaby binary star, 70 Oph AB. They didn't find any, which can seem like a failure. But in this case, their work only ruled out large, Jupiter-mass planets at certain distances. There could still be Earth-sized planets there, and their precise findings will only fuel a deeper search with more powerful telescopes.

articles.title: New alloy design strategy combines strength and ductility by timing hardening mechanisms
articles.description: Structural metals used in engineering projects are expected to have both high strength and high ductility: the ability to withstand heavy loads and deform before failure. Achieving both of these properties at the same time, however, is challenging.

articles.title: Light and ultrasound reveal renewable routes to compounds for pharmaceutical research
articles.description: Sustainable packaging is only the beginning. What a medicine is made from—and how its ingredients are produced—matters just as much. Yet the synthesis of compounds for pharmaceutical research can still depend on fossil feedstocks, high temperatures, strong oxidants and metals that raise costs and complicate purification. Two recently published studies from Colmenares' group at IPC PAS demonstrate that cleaner chemistry can begin at the level of a single chemical bond. The studies are published in the journal Ultrasonics Sonochemistry and Chemistry—A European Journal.

articles.description: MIT researchers have built SANDO, a flight planner that steers drones through unmapped spaces around moving obstacles it can’t predict, backed by a mathematical proof that the path stays collision-free.

articles.title: The force behind our strength: How mechanical processes regulate muscle development
articles.description: Skeletal muscles grow and regenerate as individual precursor cells—called myoblasts—fuse into long fibers from which mature muscle fibers develop. How they coordinate this process and form functional muscles is not yet fully understood. A research team at the Max-Planck-Zentrum für Physik und Medizin (MPZPM) has now shown that mechanical stress influences the fusion of muscle cells.

articles.title: AI and wastewater DNA-based mapping help identify sewer pipes at risk of corrosion
articles.description: Underground sewers that safely manage wastewater are essential to modern cities. However, since they are buried underground and difficult to access, their condition can be hard to monitor. Traditional camera inspections are costly and time-consuming, but we need regular inspections so aging pipes do not continue to deteriorate until they reach a breaking point. When damaged pipes leak, they can pose serious risks to public health by contaminating surrounding water, while more severe failures can even damage infrastructure above them, causing sinkholes in city streets.

articles.title: STAT+: RevMed’s pancreatic cancer drug nears European approval
articles.description: Following a green light from the FDA, European regulators have now recommended the approval of Revolution Medicines' Rasonque for pancreatic cancer.

articles.title: Shredded star reveals a massive black hole wandering far from its galaxy's center
articles.description: Astronomers have discovered a star being torn apart by a massive black hole more than 1,000 parsecs from the center of its host galaxy. The tidal disruption event, TDE 2023mfm, was first discovered by ZTF and then studied with a wide range of telescopes, including Keck, Lick, Hubble, Swift, Chandra, XMM-Newton and the VLA. The discovery paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 28.

articles.title: What exactly is a Hi-Fi listening bar?
articles.description: Forget shouting over the music. At a Hi-Fi listening bar, you’re actually there to listen. Born in Japan and now popping up around the world, the concept puts vinyl, carefully tuned sound systems and intimate, low-lit spaces at the heart of a night out. At Saikindō in Abu Dhabi, the experience doesn’t stop at what comes through the speakers. Its cocktail menu takes songs apart and translates them into flavors you can drink. We spend a day there with Beverage Director and DJ Marco Corallo to find out why the world is tuning into listening bars, and what a favorite song might taste like in a glass.

articles.title: NASA captures strange waves high above Hurricane Simon
articles.description: As Hurricane Simon unleashed destructive winds and flooding along Mexico’s coast, NASA satellites captured an extraordinary sight: massive atmospheric waves rippling high above the storm. The rare images reveal how powerful hurricanes can disturb the upper atmosphere, creating patterns that are usually invisible from space.

articles.title: Performance under pressure: A new perspective on why we fail—or rise to the occasion
articles.description: The decisive penalty kick in a final, match point in tennis or the last attempt in a competition: When a lot is at stake, even a well-practiced performance can suddenly break down. Yet pressure does not necessarily impair performance. Some people perform at their best precisely in the moments that matter most. Existing accounts can only partly explain why.

articles.description: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.

articles.description: Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest winter maximum in 2026, extending a remarkable decline that began after years of record-breaking growth. Scientists are investigating whether the dramatic reversal signals a long-term shift in Antarctica's frozen landscape.

articles.title: Can extra weight weigh on your dog's brain?
articles.description: Scientists have learned a lot about what happens to the human body as we age. But there's still much to learn about how other species age, including dogs. Even carrying extra weight could affect a dog's cognitive health. Alexandra Genualdi, a student at Oklahoma State University who presented her research in September at the American Physiological Society's 2026 Comparative Physiology conference in Orlando, talks about her efforts to learn more.

articles.title: Newly discovered viruses reveal an evolutionary missing link
articles.description: Researchers at the University of Miami have identified a group of previously unknown viruses that bridge an evolutionary gap between viruses and cellular protein compartments, a discovery with implications for both biotechnology and scientists' understanding of the origins of life.

articles.title: Human gut-inspired biobattery delivers 0.75 volts for 14 hours in US lab tests
articles.description: US researchers develop a gut-inspired biobattery that generates 0.75 volts using bacteria embedded in flexible hydrogel.

articles.title: Food, fear and physics help explain group behavior from plankton to whales
articles.description: The open ocean is a dynamic environment, where food is patchy, predators are plentiful, and oceanographic conditions change constantly. Life in the pelagic environment—the offshore waters that extend from the sunlit surface through the twilight zone—requires unique adaptations for survival.

articles.title: AI turns scrap impurities into useful ingredients for stronger recycled iron
articles.description: About 2 billion metric tons of metal are produced worldwide every year to meet the demands of industry, infrastructure and the energy sector. Much of this production still relies on primary raw materials, contributing to an estimated 40% of industrial greenhouse gas emissions and 10% of global energy consumption. Increasing the use of recycled metals could significantly reduce the environmental impact of metal production while also lowering dependence on imports of scarce and strategically critical raw materials.

articles.title: The little‑known 14th-century battle that has shaped English, Scottish and French relations
articles.description: On Oct. 17, 1346, the Battle of Neville's Cross was fought outside Durham in the northeast of England. It was a decisive moment in Anglo-Scottish history that led to the capture of King David II of Scotland. Yet few have heard of it.

articles.title: North Sea heat wave fueled underwater plankton bloom largely missed by satellites
articles.description: When a marine heat wave strikes, scientists often turn to satellites to see how the ocean is responding. From space, changes in ocean color can reveal shifts in phytoplankton, microscopic organisms that form the foundation of marine food webs and play a crucial role in the global carbon cycle. But satellites have a fundamental limitation: they can only see the ocean's surface.
